'Sarika, hi. I got us both cold coffee.'
'I only have twenty minutes.'
'That's fine.' Lavanya sat across from her in the college canteen they used to skip lectures in. 'You look tired.'
'I'm fine. We're doing important work.'
'I believe you. What kind of work?'
'You wouldn't understand. People outside are asleep.'
Lavanya took a sip and let that sit. She wanted to say, That's a line, you didn't used to talk like this. She didn't. 'Okay. Maybe I don't understand. I'd like to.'
'That's what they said you'd do. Act interested.'
'I'm not acting. I miss you. That's all.'
Sarika looked at the table. Her thumb rubbed the edge of the cup.
'I have to go.'
'Okay. Same time next month? I'll bring the coffee.'
Sarika hesitated at the door. 'Maybe.'
Lavanya watched her go and didn't follow.

qa.a: It keeps trust alive, so when Sarika's doubts grow she will have someone safe to come back to.

qa.a: It suggests she may be more unsettled than her stock replies show, perhaps moved by being missed.

The first time I tried to talk to Shreya about the group, I made a mess of it. I said, 'Beta, these people are using you.' She stood up, said, 'Mummy, you sound exactly like they said you would,' and left. She didn't call for two months.
I'm her mother. I wanted to argue, to send articles, to cry at her. My sister told me to threaten to cut her off.
I didn't. I sent a message every Sunday instead. Nothing heavy. 'Made your favourite rasam today.' 'The neem tree is flowering.' She read them. She didn't reply.
When she did come home for Diwali, I didn't bring it up. When she said something that sounded like a slogan, I said, 'Hm. Tell me more,' and meant it.
She's still with them. But last week she asked, very quietly, if her old room was still there.
It is. I told her so.
— Manjula

First visit, October. Vasudha travelled to the group's centre with Aditi's favourite pickle. Aditi met her at the gate and said, "Amma, I'm happy. You're seeing through fear." The same sentence, twice. Vasudha wanted to shout. She said, "Okay. I just wanted to see your face," and left the pickle.
Second visit, January. When Vasudha asked gently about Aditi's old job, Aditi's jaw tightened. "Outsiders always ask about money." Vasudha kept her voice soft. "I asked because I miss hearing about your work. That's all."
Third contact, April. Aditi phoned late at night, voice thin. She didn't say much. She asked whether her room at home was still the same. Vasudha said, "Exactly the same. Your books are waiting." She didn't ask a single question. After they hung up, Vasudha sat in the dark, shaking, and let herself hope.

Nandini, your friend won't listen right now, and that hurts. Let me tell you about my friend Geeta. We were twenty-four, sharing a flat in Mumbai, when she joined a group that met every night in a rented hall.
Every time I asked something, she gave me the same line: "You wouldn't understand, Simran, you're still asleep." Once I lost my temper and called the leader a fraud. She moved out that week.
After that I changed. I sent her a postcard every month, small things, the monsoon, a film I'd seen. I never mocked her group again. When we met by chance at the station, she was stiff and defensive. I just said, "I'm glad to see you. My door is open."
Three years later, at eleven one night, she rang my bell with one bag. The first thing she said was, "You never laughed at me."

qa.q: What did Simran send Geeta every month?
qa.a: A postcard, small things.

qa.q: What did young Simran feel when Geeta repeated 'you're still asleep'?
qa.a: Simran felt hurt and angry, enough to lose her temper once and call the leader a fraud.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story mattered most?
qa.a: Stopping the mocking and sending monthly postcards, which kept trust alive so Geeta knew where to go when she was ready.

qa.q: What did Simran's calm mean to Geeta when she finally left?
qa.a: It meant safety; Geeta felt she could come back without shame because Simran had never laughed at her.

grounding: An elder recalls meeting a friend's stock replies, dropping ridicule and keeping the door open, which mattered when doubt grew.

Tarun had ten minutes. Nirmala's group was changing trains at Nagpur at 6 a.m., and she had texted him just once: the platform number. It was her first message in eight months.
He found her on platform 4 among a dozen people in matching grey shawls, a leader watching from the bench. She hugged him stiffly.
"You look thin," he said, then regretted it.
"I've never been better. The world outside is lost, Tarun." She said it the way you'd read from a card.
He wanted to argue. He wanted to take her bag and walk her out through the station gate. Instead he pressed a packet of her favourite chikki into her hand. "Just so you have it. My number hasn't changed. Any time, any hour."
The train horn went. She glanced at the leader, then back at him, and for half a second her face softened. Then she was gone into the crowd.

qa.q: Which platform was Nirmala on?
qa.a: Platform 4.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Nirmala gave her stock reply?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and desperate, wanting to argue or pull her away, but held back to keep her trust.

qa.q: Why are the chikki and the reminder about his number a wise choice?
qa.a: They show care without ridicule or pressure, leaving a clear, safe door open for when her doubt grows.

qa.q: What might Nirmala have felt when her face softened?
qa.a: She may have felt a flicker of longing and doubt, touched by his kindness despite the leader watching.

grounding: In a rushed ten-minute meeting a friend meets a stock reply, stays calm and leaves the door open without ridicule.

Growth is tiring," Farida replied, as if reading from a card. Elizabeth asked about the weekend sessions. "People who aren't inside can't judge it." Elizabeth's cheeks burned. Farida looked at her for a second, then down at her phone. "I have to go." Elizabeth nodded. "Same place next month? No questions, just chai." Farida didn't answer, but she didn't say no.
